notes: Mendeley Data hpfv67fgb8 version 1 (2025-10-10, Daffodil International University). Barishal-dialect Bengali, 5 emotions (Affection, Happiness, Jealousy, Normal, Sadness). The description promises 16 kHz WAV, a train/val split and a CSV (speaker, duration), but the release is 2,312 m4a files (AAC etc.) in emotion folders with no split and no CSV. "Five native Barishal speakers (aged 22-45, gender-balanced) collected samples" can mean they spoke or that they collected. On listening, all clips sound like the same (child-like) female voice, and a speaker model (ESPnet-SPK SKA-TDNN trained on VoxCeleb; EER 24% on the reference SUBESCO) puts 2,204 of 2,303 clips (96%) in one cluster. The 99 outliers (70 of them normal) were not listened to. No voice difference between emotions could be heard, and transcripts show the sentence content itself expresses the emotion (e.g. sadness: "the happy days are over"; affection: "don't look at your phone while eating"). Therefore not used. The speaker and content checks were provisional and of low reliability (2026-10-23). Whisper language ID also gives mostly bn (94% of the 682 clips with confidence >= 0.9).

Notes: Each emotion category is performed using a different emotion-specific script, creating a deterministic correspondence between lexical content and emotion labels. notes: Wu, Nafziger, Scodary, Maas (Gridspace and Stanford). 1,446 simulated call-centre calls, 59 speakers (in agent and caller roles). One call = 2 wav files (one per side, 8 kHz mono PCM_16). Human transcripts by trained Gridspace Mixer workers. Segmentation follows the word times of Gridspace's automatic speech recognition (paper: "automatic segmentation"). In all 25,730 segments `duration_ms` matches the end of the last word of the machine transcript. Measured disagreements with the README: `duration_ms` is described as the call length but is the segment length; `offset_ms` does not match the audio position (`start_ms` does); `channel_index` (1 = caller, 2 = agent) and `speaker_role` are swapped in 37 calls (596 segments), and the voice is in the wav on the `channel_index` side (confirmed by listening and audio energy). Differences from Table 1 of the paper: words per utterance, paper mean 4.1 and median 4.5, measured (`human_transcript`) mean 5.64 and median 4.0; utterances per call, paper 2-60, measured 3-76 (the mean 17.79 matches). `hours_reported` 23.7 corresponds to the one-side total (measured 23.655 h); both sides total 47.311 h and segments total 12.024 h. 349 segments have an empty human transcript and 5,925 only tags such as `[noise]`. The corpus has no speaker gender, age or other attributes. Simulated calls (crowd workers phoning from scripts), with vocabulary limited to about 700 words: scripted, acted conversation rather than real customers' emotions. Labels are the output of Gridspace's automatic model, not human, and no human verification is described (neither the paper nor the README gives the model's name, version, training data or accuracy). Whether to use it for training or only for evaluation is the recipe side's (maintainer's) decision, still open.

GitHub Issue #9 reports audio disturbances affecting roughly 200 training videos (especially files larger than 2.5 MB) and multiple video-text mismatch or synchronization errors. label_basis_note: Label = the majority of three annotators (graduate students) who judged each utterance with the video clip available (Section 3.1; Fleiss kappa 0.43). The original EmotionLines annotation had only the transcripts. The labels therefore are not judgements of the voice alone.
lexical_confound_note: Emotion labels come from annotators who understood the words and saw the video (and the original EmotionLines labels came from transcripts alone), so the wording of an utterance probably carries information about its label. Not measured.
source_rights_note: Clips of the TV series Friends. The GPL-3.0 license in the repository covers the authors' work and the README states no rights for the material. Notes: SUBESCO is an audio-only emotional speech corpus of 7000 sentence-level utterances of the Bangla language. 20 professional actors (10 males and 10 females) participated in the recordings of 10 sentences for 7 target emotions. The emotions are Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happiness, Neutral, Sadness and Surprise. Total duration of the corpus is 7 hours 40 min 40 sec.  Total size of the dataset is 2.03 GB. The dataset was evaluated by 50 raters (25 males, 25 females). Human perception test achieved a raw accuracy of 71%.  All the details relating to creation, evaluation and analysis of SUBESCO have been described in the corresponding journal paper which has been published in Plos One.
label_basis_note: Label = the target emotion in the file name. A perception test with 50 raters (25 male, 25 female) is reported with a raw accuracy of 71% (Zenodo record); the raters' answers are not distributed.
lexical_confound_note: Ten sentences spoken in all seven emotions by every speaker (the sentences are listed in the paper), so the words carry no label information.
human_accuracy_note: 50 raters (25 male, 25 female) in a perception test of the whole corpus; raw accuracy 71% (chance 0.143). Only the aggregate is published.
status_note: Implemented with 7 classes (angry / disgust / fear / happy / neutral / sad / surprise); uses 6,969 of the 7,000 clips. Left out: 31 groups of the same recording (the maintainer listened and confirmed, 2026-10-26; the first by name is kept). 724 stereo files with an almost silent right channel are read from the left channel only.
notes: SUST Bangla Emotional Speech Corpus (SUBESCO), PLOS One 2021 (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0250173), Zenodo 4526477. 20 professional actors (10 male, 10 female), 10 sentences, 7 emotions, 5 takes: 7,000 wav (44.1 kHz 4,555 files, 48 kHz 2,445; 724 of them stereo with right channel about -81 dB against -13 dB on the left), total 7.83 h measured (the Zenodo text says 7 h 40 min 40 s). The release has 6,001 wav files (the paper says 6,000; reads as a one-off from the generation script's stop condition, but that is a guess). 16 kHz mono 16-bit, 0.819-30.506 s, 11.1437 h in total, 6 voices. The paper's listening test (20 people, forced choice) gives neutral .6, happiness .35, sadness .5, anger .55 (mean .5): hard for people to tell apart. Voice genders disagree between sources (paper and `db.yaml` vs the GitHub script), so none are given. The Zenodo description says "three basic emotions", but the paper and release have 5 + neutral, 6 classes. The maintainer's assessment: quite poor synthetic data; unsure whether to use it in experiments (2026-10-20).

Notes: These stimuli were modeled on the Northwestern University Auditory Test No. 6 (NU-6; Tillman & Carhart, 1966). notes: Thai SER corpus (arXiv 2507.09618): 27,854 recordings (41.6 h), 100 recording sessions (studio 80: soundproof 18 and ordinary room 62; Zoom 20), scripted and improvisation sessions, 200 professional actors (18-55 years) directed by students, graduates and staff of an arts faculty of Chulalongkorn University. Labels are the crowd majority, not the instruction. Agreement (the share of votes on the majority emotion) is stored per recording in the data; the paper recommends removing agreement below 0.71 (alpha 0.692, the smallest threshold that gives alpha at least 0.667); in version 2.0 this keeps 14,181 recordings (14,182 in version 1). Not used: 2,664 recordings with no majority (None) and 5 'other', and the studio clip and middle microphone channels. Of the 25,185 used, 16,491 (65%) have a majority equal to the instruction; for agreement of at least 0.71 it is 10,942 of 14,181 (77%) and below it 5,549 of 11,004 (50%). Share kept at 0.71 per emotion: frustrated 44%, neutral 57%, sad 57%, angry 63%, happy 73%. Three byte-identical pairs (same label): s001_con_actor002_impro1_25/_28, s048_con_actor136_impro6_9/_10, s078_con_actor195_impro12_7/_8. The longest recording is 108.8 s. No checksums published.
